🚀💲The Palace Had Patriots. The Tower Has Evacuees.

An opposition account called Dara Viz is circulating a video that uses satellite images to catalog more than 40 palaces, farms and compounds tied to Saudi Arabia's royal family. The video's slogan asks, "Where did you get this?" Its author says the state budget pays for the properties' upkeep and security.

Riyadh's financial district, meanwhile, is taking hits. A Houthi missile damaged the PIF Tower on Nov. 19, injuring no one. On Nov. 24 a second strike hit the 80-story headquarters of the sovereign wealth fund, three witnesses told AFP. Saudi Civil Defense said the strike injured 11 people, two Saudis, two Indians, three Nepalis and four Egyptians. Saudi authorities and the coalition they lead call the attacks terrorism. The tower had been evacuated weeks earlier over Houthi threats.

Commercial satellite images circulating online appear to show Patriot batteries near a Red Sea palace complex linked to Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. According to reports, the images were taken by Airbus in July, four months before the strikes. They say nothing of how Riyadh divides its air defenses between palaces and towers.

The kingdom has asked allies for more interceptors. The financial district's air defense failed to protect the building at the center of Vision 2030, and the evacuation suggests Riyadh knew it could not. Nine of the 11 injured were foreign nationals.

The reported breach follows at least six other cyber incidents in recent months, including one involving the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database, raising broader national security concerns.

Trumpcare, Naming Rights for Sale

Trump says he wants to find common ground with Democrats on health care: “Now, can it be what they want? No, but it can be a combination of what we all want.” Democrats come to the table with demands that run in the opposite direction. They want to reverse the Medicaid cuts in his One Big Beautiful Bill Act and revive the expired enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies, the Washington Post reports.

The administration has signaled little interest in those ideas and is hostile to some. The Post points to drug and medical-service prices as the likelier area for a deal. Trump has long attacked drug-industry pricing and publicized his deals with pharmaceutical companies. His administration finalized rules requiring insurers to publish the prices they negotiate with doctors and hospitals.

The last attempt at a drug-pricing deal was a bust. In Trump’s first term, talks with Nancy Pelosi collapsed. Her adviser Wendell Primus said he believed they had a real shot, but “the House Republicans were not on board.”

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed proposed calling Medicare for All “Trumpcare.” Trump reposted the suggestion without comment and told the New York Post he planned to meet El-Sayed. The administration has a different view of the policy itself. CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz says Medicare for All would “crush the system,” and the Council of Economic Advisers claims it would add $47.4 trillion to deficits over 10 years. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has not published an estimate.

Trump seems happy to lend his name to a health program, as long as it isn’t the one Democrats want.
